You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

=== EXTRACTED CLINICAL ENTITIES — YOU MUST RETAIN ALL OF THESE ===
Patient: male | Age: 42
Primary Diagnosis: Abdominal sepsis associated with acute on chronic kidney disease
  Secondary: Crohn's disease
  Secondary: Post-ileocolectomy status
  Secondary: Acute perforative abdomen (recent history)
  Secondary: Intra-abdominal collection (recent history)
Symptoms at admission: Hypotension (low blood pressure); Fever; Fainting; Abdominal sepsis signs
Anomalies/Findings:
  [ABNORMAL] Hypotension = Borderline blood pressure (normal: 120/80 mmHg)
  [ABNORMAL] Fever (normal: 36.5 - 37.5 °C)
  [CRITICAL] Acute on chronic kidney disease (normal: Creatinine 0.6-1.2 mg/dL (approx))
Procedures performed:
  • Ileocolectomy and creation of new anastomosis
  • Transfer to Intensive Care Unit (ICU) on 26/12/2021
Medications:
  • Vancomycin — Strong antibiotic to fight the infection.
  • Meropenem — Strong antibiotic to fight the infection.
  • KCl 6% — Potassium supplement to keep heart and muscles working properly. | Dosage: Orally
  • Loperamide — Medicine to stop diarrhea. | Dosage: Continuous
  • Calcium carbonate — Calcium supplement for bones and to help with digestion. | Dosage: Continuous
  • Cholestyramine — Medicine to bind bile and help with diarrhea. | Dosage: Continuous
  • Muciloid — Medicine to soothe the gut lining. | Dosage: Continuous
  • Ertapenem — Antibiotic previously prescribed for 4 weeks. | Dosage: 1 g/day, intramuscularly
Warning signs to mention:
  ⚠ Return if fever returns
  ⚠ Return if fainting or dizziness occurs
  ⚠ Return if abdominal pain worsens
  ⚠ Return if ostomy output changes significantly
Follow-up appointment: Follow-up appointment on 12/27/2021
Follow-up appointment: Scheduled hospitalization on 01/22
Ongoing treatment: Antibiotic therapy (Vancomycin/Meropenem)
Ongoing treatment: Potassium replacement
Ongoing treatment: Management of Crohn's disease medications
Hospital stay duration: 23 hours
Outcome: alive
=================================================================
CRITICAL RETENTION RULE: Every entity, value, measurement, date, medication name, finding, and recommendation listed above MUST appear in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. For any measurement (e.g. BP, blood sugar, heart rate, lab values), briefly state what the normal range is and whether the patient's value was within it.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (a machine that cleaned the blood when the kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.
13. CRITICAL — ENTITY RETENTION: Every diagnosis, medication name, procedure, anomaly value, lab result, date, and follow-up instruction listed in the extracted entities block above MUST be explicitly mentioned in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

output_text:
Your 42-year-old male family member was admitted to the hospital on 26/12/2021 for an emergency stay that lasted 23 hours. He was brought in because of abdominal sepsis (a serious infection in the belly area) which was associated with acute on chronic kidney disease (a sudden worsening of long-term kidney problems). He has a history of Crohn's disease (a condition that causes inflammation in the digestive tract) and is post-ileocolectomy status (meaning he has previously had surgery to remove part of the intestine). Recently, he had an acute perforative abdomen (a hole in the intestine) and an intra-abdominal collection (a pocket of fluid or pus in the belly), for which he underwent an ileocolectomy and creation of a new anastomosis (a surgical connection to join the remaining parts of the intestine together).

When he arrived, he had hypotension (low blood pressure), which was borderline compared to the normal range of 120/80 mmHg. He also had a fever, which is higher than the normal body temperature range of 36.5 to 37.5 °C, and he experienced fainting. His kidneys were critically affected, indicated by abnormal creatinine levels, which are normally around 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL. He was transferred to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) on 26/12/2021 for close monitoring.

To treat the infection, he was given strong antibiotics: Vancomycin and Meropenem. He is also receiving KCl 6% (a potassium supplement) orally to keep his heart and muscles working properly. For his ongoing management, he is taking several continuous medications: Loperamide to stop diarrhea, Calcium carbonate for bone health and digestion, Cholestyramine to bind bile and help with diarrhea, and Muciloid to soothe the gut lining. Previously, he was prescribed Ertapenem, an antibiotic, at a dosage of 1 g/day given intramuscularly for 4 weeks.

He is currently alive and has been discharged. You must keep him on antibiotic therapy with Vancomycin and Meropenem, continue the potassium replacement, and manage his Crohn's disease medications as directed. Please take him for a follow-up appointment on 12/27/2021. He is also scheduled for hospitalization on 01/22.

Please return to the hospital immediately if you notice any of these warning signs: if his fever returns, if he experiences fainting or dizziness, if his abdominal pain worsens, or if his ostomy output changes significantly.
